corrected_value.title_o: Happiness and Time Preference: The Effect of Positive Affect in a Random-Assignment Experiment

decisions.quote: Experimental Economics Replication Project Replication of Happiness and Time Preference: The Effect of Positive Affect in a Random-Assignment Experiment by Ifcher, J./Zarghamee, H. (2011) in: The American Economic Review, 101(7), pp. 3109–3129. Replication Authors: Colin Camerer, Taisuke Imai, Gidi Nave Ifcher and Zarghamee study the causal effect of a mood-inducing film clip on time preference. They conclude that exposure to a positive-affect inducing film increases patience (measured by p/m, where p is the present value of a reward m available in the future). Hypothesis to bet on: Showing subjects a film clip inducing positive affect will increase measured patience, excluding subjects who do not discount at all (Table 3, column 5).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ifcher and Zarghamee (2011), header and introduction (line 1332); Reference 46 (lines 312-313); Table S1 (line 1268)
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 2099 and blind target 13 identify the same tested original study: Ifcher and Zarghamee (2011), 'Happiness and Time Preference: The Effect of Positive Affect in a Random-Assignment Experiment', American Economic Review, 101(7), 3109-3129 (DOI 10.1257/aer.101.7.3109), which is directly replicated in the individual primary report and listed as Reference 46 in the main manuscript.

decisions.quote: Discussion Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has not been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%. The relative effect size equals -1.90% and the p-value of the hypothesis test is 0.993. The original result testing the joint hypothesis of happiness induction and induced happiness changing time preference is not replicated: a film clip which induced positive affect in the original study did not increase measured patience using the planned statistical test.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ifcher and Zarghamee (2011), Discussion section, p. 3/6 (line 1332); Table S1 (line 1268)
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind code the outcome as 'failed'. In the individual primary replication report for Ifcher and Zarghamee (2011), the authors explicitly state the overall verdict that the hypothesis of interest was not replicated (treatment effect coefficient = -0.057, p = 0.933 in Table 1 / p = 0.993 in Discussion text, relative effect size = -1.90%, and Table S1 'Replicated = No'). In addition, the mood-induction manipulation check and supplementary regressions correcting for self-reported mood induction also failed to support the original effect. Under codebook Rule 1, the authors' explicit overall verdict of non-replication governs.

decisions.quote: Differences from Original Study The replication procedure is identical to that of the original study, with some unavoidable deviations and a difference in payment procedure. The subject pools are likely to be somewhat different. Collecting the same demographic data, and performing the analysis which uses these covariates, should help reduce any such effects. The replication will be performed on students and non-students from the Nuffield College (Oxford, UK) subject pool, while the original data was gathered at Santa Clara University. The experiment will be in English as in the original study. Replication Results The total of 168 subjects participated in the replication experiments (86 in the positive mood treatment and 82 in the neutral treatment), of which 131 discounted.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ifcher and Zarghamee (2011), Differences from Original Study and Replication Results sections, pp. 2/6-3/6 (line 1332)
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind code the record type as 'replication'. The study collected new experimental data in an independent sample (168 participants, 131 discounters, from the Nuffield College Oxford subject pool) to re-test the published finding of Ifcher and Zarghamee (2011).

decisions.quote: Experimental Economics Replication Project Replication of A Continuous Dilemma by Friedman, D./Oprea, R. (2012) in: The American Economic Review, 102(1), pp. 337–363. Replication Authors: Colin Camerer, Taisuke Imai, Gidi Nave Friedman and Oprea look at cooperation in a prisoner’s dilemma comparing a treatment with continuous time with flow payoffs over 60 seconds to a treatment with eight equal subperiods. Cooperation is higher under continuous time. Hypothesis to bet on: Cooperation in the prisoner’s dilemma is higher in continuous time with flow payoffs over 60 seconds compared to eight equal subperiods (a comparison in the level of cooperation between the continuous treatment and the grid-8 treatment).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Friedman and Oprea (2012), header and introduction (line 1322); Reference 43 (line 307); Table S1 (line 1265)
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 2100 and blind target 10 identify the same tested original study: Friedman and Oprea (2012), 'A Continuous Dilemma', American Economic Review, 102(1), 337-363 (DOI 10.1257/aer.102.1.337), which is directly replicated in the individual primary report and listed as Reference 43 in the main manuscript.

decisions.quote: In the replication experiments, the median cooperation rate in continuous treatment is 0.504 compared to 0.000 in grid-8 treatment. A Mann-Whitney test applied to by-subject median cooperation rates yields statistically significant difference with a p-value equal to 0.004. Similar to the original study, the higher cooperation rate was achieved under continuous-time treatment. The original effect size is 0.893 − 0.250 = 0.743 (the difference in cooperation rates between continuous and grid-8). The replication effect size 2/3 Experimental Economics Replication Project is 0.504 − 0.000 = 0.504. Therefore, the relative effect size is 0.504/0.743 = 67.83%. Unplanned Protocol Deviations The replication experiments were conducted exactly in the way as described above without any deviations from the protocol. Discussion Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%. The relative effect size equals 67.83% and the p-value of the hypothesis test is 0.004.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Friedman and Oprea (2012), Replication Results and Discussion sections, pp. 2/3-3/3 (line 1322); Table S1 (line 1265)
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind code the outcome as 'successful'. The individual primary replication report for Friedman and Oprea (2012) explicitly concludes that the hypothesis of interest was replicated at alpha < 5% (Mann-Whitney p = 0.004, median cooperation 0.504 in continuous vs. 0.000 in Grid-8, relative effect size 67.83%), and Table S1 marks 'Replicated = Yes'. Under codebook Rule 1, this explicit overall verdict governs.

decisions.quote: Differences from Original Study The replication procedure is identical to that of the original study, with some unavoidable deviations. This replication will be performed at the National University of Singapore in Singapore, in 2015, on undergraduate students from the National University of Singapore, while the original data was gathered at the University of California, Santa Cruz, USA, in 2009, on undergraduate students from all major disciplines at the University of California, Santa Cruz. The experiment will be in English as in the original study. The original study also looks at a One-Shot treatment, but the focus of the replication is on the difference between continuous and grid8 treatments. Replication Results The total of 40 subjects (20 in continuous treatment and 20 in grid-8 treatment) participated in replication experiment.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Friedman and Oprea (2012), Differences from Original Study and Replication Results sections, p. 2/3 (line 1322)
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind code the record type as 'replication'. The study collected new experimental data in an independent sample (40 undergraduate students at the National University of Singapore) to re-test the published finding of Friedman and Oprea (2012).
